107-r1.locator: §5 'Block Walking and the Explicit Formula', pp. 5-6 (reflection principle; Theorem 3 and Corollary 1)
107-r1.proofSketch: Count monotone N/E walks with n N's and n E's that never have more E's than N's. Total walks number $\binom{2n}{n}$, so subtract the bad walks. For a bad walk, find the first step at which E's outnumber N's; interchange N and E in the segment up to and including that step. The result has $n+1$ N's and $n-1$ E's, and the map is reversible (first time N's exceed E's), so bad walks are in bijection with all walks in an $(n-1)\times(n+1)$ grid. Hence $C_n=\binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n-1}=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$.

107-r3.proofSketch: Show that triangulations of a polygon with $n+2$ sides (into $n$ triangles) satisfy the Catalan recursion. Fix a side as the base; in any triangulation it lies in exactly one triangle, the base triangle. That triangle splits the polygon into two smaller triangulated polygons, with $k+2$ sides on one side and $n-k+1$ sides on the other, with $k$ running over $0,\dots,n-1$ (extreme values when the base triangle uses two polygon edges). Hence $T_n=\sum_k T_kT_{n-1-k}$ with the same initial values, so $T_n=C_n$.

107-r2.sourceTitle: MAT344 Lecture 5 (Univ. of Toronto, Summer 2019) and R. P. Stanley, Catalan Numbers (CUP 2015), Chapter 1 excerpt
107-r2.locator: Toronto MAT344 Lecture 5, §3 Recursion, p. 2 (first-return decomposition giving C_n=sum C_{k-1}C_{n-k}); Stanley, Catalan Numbers, Ch. 1, §1.3 Prop. 1.3.1 (gf from recurrence 1.1) and §1.4 Thm 1.4.1 proof, pp. 3-5 (CUP free excerpt https://assets.cambridge.org/97811070/75092/excerpt/9781107075092_excerpt.pdf)
107-r2.proofSketch: Take a nonempty Dyck path and look at the first time after the initial up step that it returns to the diagonal, at $(k,k)$. Removing the first and last steps of the initial excursion leaves a Dyck path of semilength $k-1$, and the remainder is a Dyck path of semilength $n-k$; thus $C_n=\sum_{k=1}^nC_{k-1}C_{n-k}$ with $C_0=1$. Multiplying the recurrence by $x^n$ and summing gives $(C(x)-1)/x=C(x)^2$, i.e. $xC^2-C+1=0$; the minus sign in the quadratic formula is forced by $C(0)=1$, so $C(x)=(1-\sqrt{1-4x})/(2x)$. Extracting coefficients with the binomial series for $(1-4x)^{1/2}$ gives $C_n=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$.

107-r4.sourceTitle: Enumerative Combinatorics 3: Catalan numbers (LTCC lecture notes)
107-r4.locator: §3.2 'Example: Catalan numbers', pp. 2-4 (bracketings, last-operation recurrence, generating function, formula) and §3.3 'Binary trees', p. 5 (Figure 1)
107-r4.proofSketch: Let $C_n$ count the bracketings of a product of $n$ terms under a non-associative operation. The last application of the operation combines a bracketed product of the first $m$ terms with one of the last $n-m$ terms, giving $C_n=\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}C_mC_{n-m}$ with $C_1=1$. Hence $c(x)=x+c(x)^2$, solved by $c(x)=\tfrac12(1-\sqrt{1-4x})$ (sign fixed by $c(0)=0$); the binomial series gives $C_n=\frac1n\binom{2n-2}{n-1}$ (i.e. $\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$ for $n+1$ terms). Binary trees with $n$ leaves are parse trees of bracketed products, so they obey the same count.
